tier_reason: The numbers come from Snellman's independent 2014 blog, which compares the Intel fork against stock zlib (baseline) and the Cloudflare fork. The blog itself is egress-blocked, so its level-1 and level-5 figures were confirmed only through WebSearch snippets. Its harness is public (github.com/jsnell/zlib-bench) but its README states no compiler, flags or CPU. A blog read only through snippets stays at C; it could reach B if the post is opened in full.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Third-party blog (Snellman 2014, read through WebSearch snippets only): at level 1, Intel's 'quick' strategy takes 36% of baseline time on an executable (Cloudflare fork 70%), but its compressed size grows to 0.46 of the original against 0.37 for baseline. At level 5 ('medium' strategy) it takes 0.99 s against a 1.76 s baseline on the executable (56% of baseline time), and 0.75 s against 0.69 s on JPEG (108%, slower on uncompressible data). Derived from page data: about 2.8x faster at level 1 and 1.8x at level 5 on the executable. The claims that levels 7-9 are slightly behind Cloudflare and that decompression is slower than Cloudflare's were not re-confirmed in this run.
corrections.caveats: The benchmark blog (snellman.net) is egress-blocked, so its figures were checked only through WebSearch snippets: level 1 at 36% of baseline time with a worse ratio (0.46 vs 0.37), and level 5 at 0.99 s vs 1.76 s on an executable and 0.75 s vs 0.69 s on JPEG. The harness is public at github.com/jsnell/zlib-bench, but its README names no compiler, flags or CPU; the i7-4770 comes from a snippet. The blog measured the 2014 state of the fork, not the later 1.2.13 rebase. The repo was archived on 2024-03-01 with Intel's 'no longer maintained' notice. Superseded by zlib-ng (already catalogued): zlib-ng's README says it has 'Deflate medium and quick algorithms based on Intel's zlib fork' and 'Includes improvements from Cloudflare and Intel forks', and its author says he 'merge[d] all the Intel optimizations'. Use zlib-ng instead; keep this entry for history and attribution. The level-1 'quick' strategy trades compression ratio for speed. The license is the standard zlib license (LICENSE file read).

notes: Superseded by zlib-ng, which merged Intel's deflate_quick and deflate_medium according to zlib-ng's README. Consider listing it as reference or history rather than a recommended pick. Metadata confirmed from github.com: archived 2024-03-01, 144 stars, 37 forks, not a GitHub fork, last commit 2024-03-01 'archive repository'.

tier_reason: Every number in the README enwik8 table matches the record. The benchmark script is public (.github/workflows/enwik8-benchmark.yml) and the build flags are given, but no CPU model is stated and the README table's machine is unnamed, so it falls short of A. The numbers are first-party, so C.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Workflow: Rust nightly via actions-rust-lang/setup-rust-toolchain, rustflags '--allow warnings -C target-feature=+aes', cargo build --release (Cargo.toml release profile: opt-level 3, lto true, codegen-units 1, overflow-checks false). Baseline tools are apt packages on ubuntu-latest (versions not pinned).
corrections.baseline: xz -6, zstd -19/-15/-10, brotli -9/-8/-7, bzip2 -9, lzfse, gzip -6 (GNU gzip CLI)
corrections.caveats: The benchmark script is public and the workflow gives the compiler and flags, but no CPU model is stated and the baseline tool versions are not pinned (apt on ubuntu-latest), so it falls short of tier A. The README table was produced on an unnamed machine and does not match the workflow's rows: the workflow runs gzip -9 and brotli -6/-9 and has no lzfse, while the README shows gzip -6, brotli -7/-8/-9 and lzfse. The gzip row is the GNU gzip CLI, not the zlib library. Only one file was tested (enwik8, English text), so the ratio claims may not hold for binary data. The baseline levels are mostly the high-ratio ones. Decoding is not a win: orz decodes in about 0.58-0.60 s against 0.08 s for zstd and 0.107 s for gzip, though it is faster than xz -6 (0.812 s) and bzip2 (1.795 s). The claim is compression speed at a matched ratio. It is a ROLZ codec with its own format, so it does not replace the zlib or zstd formats. Same author as libzling.

notes: The README table matches the record exactly, and the derived ratios check out (44.936/3.360 = 13.4x; size is 0.85% larger). Metadata from github.com: 817 stars, 50 forks, MIT/Apache-2.0, latest tag v1.6.2, last commit 2026-03-18, active.

tier_reason: The author's page (create.stephan-brumme.com/smallz4) is egress-blocked. WebSearch snippets confirm an enwik9 comparison against lz4 -9, but the machine, compiler and method are unseen, so this is first-party data without methodology: C. The output-size gain is only 0.86% with no speed win, so it is a niche optimal-parse entry.

corrections.claimed_speedup: No compression-speed win; it is an optimal-parse LZ4 encoder for slightly smaller output. WebSearch snippets of the author's page and an encode.su thread give, on enwik9: lz4 r128 -9 at 374,905,570 bytes and smallz4 0.5 -9 at 371,681,075 bytes (derived from page data: 0.86% smaller). One snippet gives smallz4 1.3 -9 at 371,680,328 bytes in 262 s. The record's 33 s (lz4) and 242 s (smallz4 0.5) timings and the lz4ultra 1.3.0 figure of 371,680,323 bytes were not re-confirmed in this run. Decoding uses the standard lz4 format, so decode speed is unchanged.
corrections.caveats: Numbers come only from WebSearch snippets of the author's site (create.stephan-brumme.com) and an encode.su thread, both egress-blocked, so the machine, CPU and compiler are unknown. The version attached to the 371,680,328-byte result conflicts between sources: a snippet says smallz4 1.3, while the original record said 1.5. The GitHub readme is two lines and calls GitHub 'a mirror only'. The Makefile uses g++ -O2 (gcc -O2 -std=c99 for smallz4cat). Not faster than the baseline at compression (about 7-8x slower than lz4 -9 per the snippet figures); it gives slightly smaller LZ4 output and has a tiny standalone decoder (smallz4cat). The GitHub mirror's last commit is 2020-04-13 ('version 1.5'); the author's site may differ.

notes: Kept as a size-only optimal-LZ4 niche entry under the seed rule. Metadata from github.com: 51 stars, 13 forks, MIT (LICENSE read), 12 commits, last 2020-04-13, so abandoned is correct. encode.su and mattmahoney.net (LTCB) are both EGRESS_BLOCKED.
